title: Bernadette at Lourdes (1858)
hookLine: a sick, poor, fourteen-year-old sees a lady in a grotto and digs where a spring appears
carry: she was only asked to tell
last: THE KING'S GOOD SERVANT, GOD'S FIRST.

cards: February 1858, a small town in the foothills of the Pyrenees. It's cold. A girl of fourteen goes out with her sister and a friend to gather firewood and bones to sell.
She's small for her age, she has asthma, and she can't read. Her family is so poor they live in one damp room that used to be the town jail. The other two cross a stream.

She hesitates at the cold water, near a rocky hollow in the cliff called Massabielle. Then she hears a sound like wind, looks up, and sees, in the grotto, a young lady dressed in white, smiling at her.

teach.h: SHE DUG, AND A SPRING CAME.
teach.b: Over that spring and summer she said the lady appeared to her eighteen times. Crowds began to follow her to the grotto. They saw nothing but a girl kneeling, her face changed.

On one visit, Bernadette said, the lady told her to drink from the spring and wash in it. There was no spring. So she scratched at the muddy ground with her hands, tried to drink the dirty water, and smeared her face.
People thought she'd lost her mind. But over the next days, water began to flow from that spot, and it still flows. Weeks later, she asked the lady her name.
The answer came in the local dialect, in words Bernadette didn't understand: I am the Immaculate Conception. She repeated them all the way to the parish priest so she wouldn't forget. He went pale.
The Pope had defined that title for Mary only four years before, and he doubted this girl had ever heard it. The police questioned her, and so did the clergy.

teach.h: ASKED TO TELL, NOT TO CONVINCE.
teach.b: She never changed her story, and she never tried to convince anyone. Her job, she said in effect, was to tell, not to make people believe. She later became a nun, suffered long illness, and died at thirty-five.
Catholics call apparitions like this private revelation: the Church approved Lourdes, but no Catholic is required to believe it.
Millions go anyway, many of them sick, to bathe in the water and to pray.

how: Catholics keep the feast of Our Lady of Lourdes on February 11, also the World Day of the Sick; millions of pilgrims visit the grotto each year, many of them ill, to pray, join the candlelight processions and bathe in the spring water.

practice: Bring to mind one person who is sick right now, in body or in mind, and see their face. Picture them the way pilgrims picture the ones they carry to Lourdes: not fixed, just held, just brought.
If you pray, you can pray for them now, maybe with a Hail Mary; if you don't, simply hold them in your attention and wish them well.

wordCard.voice: Massabielle. The grotto where a poor, sick girl saw a lady in white, and dug for a hidden spring.

orig.note: the lady's words in Bernadette's local Gascon dialect (not Latin, not French): I am the Immaculate Conception.
